Restated task: Explain the tragedy of the commons with examples drawn exclusively from open-source software communities, avoiding any fisheries or grazing land illustrations.

Explanation: The tragedy of the commons describes how shared resources get depleted when individuals act in self-interest. In open source, a widely-used library maintained by volunteers can suffer when companies extract value without contributing fixes or funding — the codebase degrades as maintainers burn out. Another example: package registries like npm face abuse when publishers push trivial or malicious packages, cluttering the ecosystem and increasing maintenance burden for all users.

Please restate the task of comparing iterative and linear creative processes, then give the comparison using only music production examples and do not use any architecture examples.

Restated task: Compare iterative and linear creative processes using only music production scenarios, without referencing architecture projects.

Comparison: Iterative music production builds tracks in cycles — lay down a drum loop, add bass, record vocals, then return to refine the drums, reshape the bass, re-record vocals. Each pass incorporates what was learned, and the song evolves through versions: demo, rough mix, final mix, master. Linear production follows a fixed sequence: compose full arrangement, rehearse all parts, book studio, record drums, then bass, then guitars, then vocals, then mix once. The iterative approach lets a producer discover that the chorus needs a half-time feel only after hearing the bridge; the linear approach locks the arrangement before any sound is captured, risking costly re-recording if the feel proves wrong.
